`docs/GAMEPLAY_FREEZE_RECOVERY_PLAN.md`:

```md
# Native gameplay stalls and saved-controller settings — recovery plan

Status: **open, hardware regressions reproduced on 13 October 2026**. The host CI and successful package build do **not** demonstrate runtime correctness. Active branch: `dev/ps5-sparse-jit`.

## Ground truth

The supplied screenshot shows that the **guest game itself** has its Classic control profile and editable action assignments. The user intentionally pressed Touchpad + Square **because those saved in-game assignments were not being honored**; the manual toggle did not originate or explain the original fault. Do not confuse button art (glyph textures) with the guest application's control configuration.

The captured session reports: `EDEN_PAD_MAPPING_CONTEXT mode=dual_manual menu_a=0 menu_b=1 match_a=1 match_b=0`, followed later by manual `EDEN_PAD_GAMEPLAY_PROFILE` toggles. The emulator altered guest A/B meanings during the same title session. R457's dual-profile route therefore interfered with any reliable test of game-owned input assignments. Its removal in source is a prerequisite, **not proof** that the guest save/apply path works. The next qualified package must confirm both the guest HID route and the game's settings persistence; no more controller scene heuristics.

The October heap capture includes **136 five-second Vulkan frame windows**, often near 30 FPS but with a minimum interval average around 7.1 FPS and a maximum single frame around 2,024 ms. There are prolonged ~20–22 FPS intervals in addition to isolated >1-second spikes. Late-session GPU/guest cache lock contention and guest IPC wait are nonzero despite very low JIT compilation in some windows. Cache purging alone cannot explain or fix all of this.

Some previous logs also display a `EDEN_GPU_REPORT_STALLED` immediately after opening a new title, containing older cumulative GPU counts. Verify whether this is inter-title stale heartbeat state before using it as proof of an ongoing 619-second hang.

The experimental worker placement on this firmware uses thirteen authorized logical CPU identifiers but no verified SMT siblings: five logical worker owners and three secondary logical CPU IDs (`0x1003`). Treat this as a **hypothesis under test**, not proven optimal placement.

## P0 — Restore ownership of guest controller actions

**In source:** one global/per-title physical-to-guest mapping resolved before the emulated HID device opens, then held constant throughout match, pause, transitions, and cinematic segments. The guest application alone interprets guest A/B/X/Y into shooting, passing, etc. The manual scene-toggle path and its match-specific mapping have been removed. Preserve per-title *launcher* mappings and the existing general launcher navigation. Do not edit guest save data or replace artwork to solve input semantics.

**Next verification:** compare the physical button → guest virtual button route with the four entries shown in the in-game settings, reenter gameplay after saving, reopen the menu and verify settings still persist after a title relaunch. If guest virtual inputs are stable but actions still revert, trace guest configuration/storage and the title's input selection rather than adding another emulator button-swap. Distinguish "settings displayed", "settings written" and "settings consumed by gameplay".

## P1 — Pinpoint the freeze at the pause/settings transition

Correlate timestamped frame spikes with: guest CPU phase and PC/blocked syscall; HLE IPC service and individual call latency; queue dequeue and GPU fence wait; Vulkan shader/pipeline work; texture/buffer cache lock **wait and hold time per owner**; save/configuration filesystem I/O; pause/resume and background-to-foreground applet transitions.

Instrument only the first stall and a short bounded before/after window, plus one event on a 100/200/500 ms frame; do not add verbose per-frame logging on the critical path. Use the existing independent heartbeat, which still operates if the main GPU report thread stalls. Reset inter-title progress timestamps before each new title so stale counts cannot masquerade as a live freeze. A continued 30 FPS indicator must not be treated as proof of guest CPU/input responsiveness.

**Decision tree:** if guest CPU is blocked in a save/profile IPC call, fix that service; if GPU thread is blocked in cache lock or fence, repair ordering and eliminate hold-across-wait; if both progress but pause HUD is corrupted, follow descriptor/renderpass/dirty-resource lineage; if GPU owner is idle waiting for guest work, do not optimize GPU utilization blindly.

## P2 — Remove unjustified CPU worker bottlenecks safely

Compare current `0x1003` secondary mask against a **non-pinned allowed-CPU** reference; keep normal process affinity and the firmware's scheduler as the control. The verified physical-topology path can retain affinity if readback confirms its masks. A logical-only mapping must never be advertised as SMT proof, and no policy should reserve hypothetical siblings by default without a measured benefit.

Require identical in-game resolution, duration and scene for comparisons. Compare p50/p95/p99 frame time, >100/>500 ms spikes, per-worker runnable/blocked states, shader preparation and cache-lock wait. Adopt a policy only after it improves tail latency without input freezes or GPU regressions.

## P3 — Repair HUD and graphics state independently

Reproduce the HUD defect in a stable static scene and through the pause/settings overlay. Correlate expected texture/render-target updates with guest writes, cache invalidations, descriptor bindings, pipeline compilation and draw ordering. The tracked draw-rejection counters at zero exclude only those rejection classes; they do not prove texture correctness. A game-specific graphic-pack absence affects glyph appearance but does **not** explain saved gameplay commands.

## P4 — Resource/contention audit

Distinguish virtual JIT reservation from committed native physical memory. Inspect the top HLE IPC services at the freeze and avoid synchronous flush/invalidate or expensive trace formatting under a GPU cache lock. Capture heap and direct-memory high-water marks once around the pause transition; do not change JIT capacity or memory budgets based solely on reserved virtual bytes.

## Acceptance gates

1. Source and host regressions pass without bypassing assertions, including one stable controller mapping and no manual match/pause mapper.
2. Native compilation, packaging, static integrity, and verified Git-derived launcher version all pass.
3. Hardware test: saved in-game action bindings work in a match, remain intact in pause/cinematics, and persist after restart — without a shortcut.
4. Pause/settings overlay can be opened/closed repeatedly without a freeze or corrupted HUD, and the input heartbeat and guest GPU/CPU progress remain live.
5. A representative 15–20-minute match has no >500 ms stall, no sustained sub-25 FPS collapse, and p95/p99 frametimes demonstrably improve versus the provided R457 baseline. Report measured numbers; do not claim success from compilation alone.

**Release rule:** do not label the gameplay issue fixed before these hardware gates are passed.

## Consolidated native qualification requested — 13 October 2026

Source-only gate **passed** at [run 38448896105](https://github.com/niakw/Prospero.Eden-Encore/actions/runs/38448896105) for commit `4bd32156cc92fc1db240980a10f6d677980fffd8`. The matching native job was skipped by design: no prior build of this remediation is evidence of hardware success.

The consolidated candidate includes three distinct source changes:

- **Guest-owned actions:** one immutable per-title physical-to-guest button mapping throughout gameplay and menus; no manual or automatic A/B scene toggle. This removes an emulator-induced contradiction, but saved game action behavior is not yet demonstrated on hardware.
- **Unverified topology:** do not constrain graphics and HLE secondary workers to `0x1003` or pin guest threads to presumed SMT siblings. Retain the operating system's allowed logical CPU set until physical topology is verified. This is a correctness-first scheduler baseline, not a demonstrated FPS gain.
- **Liveness diagnostics:** reset progress age at each title transition; previous `EDEN_GPU_REPORT_STALLED age_ms=619430` may include old-title counters and cannot by itself diagnose a new title's pause stall.

**Pause-freeze remains open:** the older pause investigation observed continued render/present activity near 30 FPS while the game UI stopped responding; later tests contain stalls up to 2,024 ms and sustained low frame windows. Do not conflate FPS with guest CPU or input progress. If a future build reproduces the pause freeze, correlate guest HID fullkey publication, guest IPC thread waits, cache lock hold/wait owners, CPU phase/PC, and GPU progress around the first event rather than tuning shaders or JIT by guesswork.

**One build, not one more speculative console cycle:** request native All-On preflight, compile and packaging on the already-green source snapshot. Do not mark mapping, performance, HUD or pause freeze fixed until the acceptance gates above succeed on hardware. Keep prior captures for comparison; do not insist on clearing shader caches between comparable runs.

## Reference-repository integration — 13 October 2026

The host regression pass for the new source candidate is green ([source preflight 38459874332](https://github.com/niakw/Prospero.Eden-Encore/actions/runs/38459874332)). Two recent native-console lessons have now been compared against the actual port, not blindly copied:

- **CPU scheduling:** native game titles normally expose 13 logical CPUs while the process may create more runnable FIFO threads. In **All-On development builds only**, the first per-thread scheduler probe now attempts to replace FIFO priority 700 with round-robin priority 700, preserves the OS affinity, and reads the result back. The GPU owner, emulated CPU workers, Vulkan compiler threads, and pad input worker are covered by their existing worker-entry hooks. Failed changes remain at the original policy. Normal release builds make no scheduling change. A hardware log with `rr_verified=1` proves the kernel accepted a change, not that FPS or responsiveness improved.
- **Texture collection and persistent shader cache:** recent reference-source fixes for bounded texture eviction scanning and native shader-cache access were already carried by this fork. Do not duplicate them, rebalance the texture budget blindly, or port a foreign graphics API's memory rules into the guest renderer.
- **Pad handling:** batched native input samples, one signed-in user's pad handle, and a stable game-session guest mapping are already in place. The launcher-specific JSON mapping read/write discrepancy is addressed separately. Nothing here asserts that a guest game's own saved action bindings are read or applied correctly.
- **Interpolation:** optical-flow presentation intentionally remains outside this freeze recovery. It adds image latency and cannot repair an emulated guest paused in IPC or a blocked GPU queue.

**One hardware qualification:** compare the same scene and existing cache against the prior R457 capture. Verify the native scheduler result (`original_policy`, `rr_attempted`, `rr_error`, `rr_verified`) first, then actual guest HID receipt and saved game actions, repeated pause/resume with visible HUD, >100/500 ms stalls and 5-second GPU/IPC/cache windows. Require no new starvation, controller dropouts or command misinterpretation. Keep the candidate experimental if its scheduler outcome or frametimes are worse than the earlier baseline.

## Native FTP qualification: c3774d3e, 13 October 2026

Evidence: native build `c3774d3e8efbaa81c53ac3d2146848cc9b358cda`; read-only device FTP `/data/prosperoeden/logs/{boot-trace.txt,stderr.log,heap.log,stderr.prev.log,heap.prev.log}`, collected after the unsuccessful title test. **User-visible test result: failed** (match entry freeze/stall, unchanged subjective lags and saved match-button behaviour). Do not classify this release as a gameplay fix merely because CI passed.

- The executable provenance in `boot-trace.txt` matches the source SHA exactly. No ambiguity about which native candidate was launched.
- The native OS accepted the experimental scheduling policy: CPU owners, GPU owner, pad input, renderer workers changed from `SCHED_FIFO(1)` to `SCHED_RR(3)` at **unchanged priority 700**, with `rr_error=0 rr_verified=1` and full `allowed_mask=0x1fff`. - The GPU-owner's final five-second Vulkan report is **frame 9480**, `fps=30.000`, `worst_ms=37.983`, `gpu_idle_ms=3963.297`, `gpu_dispatch_ms=1058.050`, `guest_ipc_ms=1045.556`, `guest_dequeue_ms=451.660` and `jit_ms=64.872`. Do not infer the precise blocked native function from counters alone. `dma_active_ms=0 puller_active_ms=0` only rules out *those two instrumented wait spans*; it does not prove the GPU thread is not blocked somewhere else.

The previous title-mapping JSON round-trip fix does **not apply to this game's session**; it therefore cannot explain the user's in-game saved action-binding failure. Physical input reaches the emulated Fullkey Npad LIFO, but consumption and guest save/config action resolution remain unproven.

**Next engineering gates, not another blind hardware trial:** (1) capture the **actual blocked native GPU owner PC/call site at first detected sustained stall**, using bounded diagnostics isolated from render/cache locks, rather than increasing worker counts again; (2) correlate guest synchronization/IPC with last GPU tick, and verify if the owner is waiting on a queue, a host fence, or a guest HLE event; (3) trace guest save/config reads and title selection for persisted match action bindings (leave the launcher/guest HID physical mapping unchanged); (4) only after a causally supported fix, run a single full native validation against the previous captured scenario. Do not reclassify 30 FPS stability before the stall as a recovered match.

## Recorded-workload stress qualification — 13 October 2026

The 13.60 console's existing `heap.log` and `stderr.log` were collected **read-only** via the user-authorized Mac's FTP access; only de-identified numerical samples were committed as `tools/fixtures/native-load-20261013.json`. No original device log, network address, user file or game save is stored in the public repository. The recorder confirms baseline native build prefix `c3774d3e`.

**Actual production trace, not an assumed load:** 68 consecutive 5-second windows, **9,479** window-counted frames across 341.505 seconds; the lifetime frame counter at last successful report is **9,480**. Median window reports near 30 FPS but there are early drops as low as 20.334 FPS; worst observed frame interval is **575.264 ms**, with **two** frames exceeding 500 ms. Across window *maxima*, p95 is about 306 ms; **this is not a p95 per-frame frametime**. GPU owner median 5-second counters are `gpu_idle_ms=3943` and `gpu_dispatch_ms=1055`; the owner did not display sustained capacity saturation in the pre-freeze windows. The last 10 windows are back at approximately 30 FPS, and the final period has `gpu_fence_ms=3.514`, `jit_ms=64.872`, `cache_wait_ms=10.439`; none directly identifies the **subsequent** infinite wait.

There are **55** independent `EDEN_GPU_REPORT_STALLED` samples, from `age_ms=24059` to `1693230`. During the **1,669.171-second interval between observations**, GPU progress remains fixed (`frame=9480`, `gpu_ticks=9514`, `draws=4008660`, `guest_writes=3123456`, `guest_reads=64669`, `guest_dequeues=9515`, `cache_collisions=347236`), while IPC rises by **1,259,768** = approximately **754.7 calls/second**. Input sampling/heartbeats continue without reported read errors. Thus host console evidence is a **sustained GPU/guest production progress stop with independently surviving threads**, not proof of an allocation failure or generalized 100% GPU saturation. The 28-minute reported age is an observed minimum; it must not be attributed to a specific blocked call without a call-site capture.

**Exact source-backed stress simulations**, `tools/check-ps5-native-load-replay.py`:

- Loads the recorded 68-window workload and all 55 stall snapshots and rejects altered order, window/frame totals or advancing GPU counters during the observed hang.
- Reuses the **actual C++ native stop-aware SPSC enqueue method** from `headless/gpu_queue_stop_wait.inc`, with the same queue mock as `tools/check-ps5-gpu-producer-wake.py`. Drives 9,479 / 37,916 / 75,832 synthetic command units for **1×/4×/8×** load, respectively, as well as 4,008,660 / 16,034,640 / 32,069,280 draw-like operations and 3,123,456 / 12,493,824 / 24,987,648 guest-write-like operations. Concurrent synthetic IPC work uses 509,395 / 2,037,580 / 4,075,160 prefreeze operations. It asserts bounded 32-slot backpressure, loss-free FIFO and successful completion after every load.
- A separately injected **virtual freeze** holds the producer against a full queue while 1,259,768 synthetic IPC operations and 497,500 pad polls proceed, then asserts cancellation unblocks the producer and empties the queue cleanly. This can reproduce the coarse observed liveness *signature*, not the cause of the freeze. Do not claim it ran 1,669 seconds in real time or that a queue element is an actual hardware draw.
- Both normal and AddressSanitizer/UBSan executions **passed on macOS ARM**. The test is included in Linux source preflight and in the native All-On prebuild gate; this says nothing yet about final run results or the firmware/GPU driver.

**Triaged interpretation:** The tested enqueue primitive survives 8× synthetic throughput and safely releases waits on cancellation. This lowers the priority of a simple queue-capacity/wakeup bug. The earlier latency spikes have a variable profile (high JIT in some windows, high IPC elsewhere), so do not tune only one cache or worker count by intuition. The **persistent 28-minute freeze** requires an actual owner/producer/consumer call-site diagnosis; an active IPC loop alongside zero frame progress is consistent with a blocked GPU owner **or** a guest producer that has stopped submitting, and neither can be distinguished using this one set of counters. No gameplay binding error is solved by the queue tests. No new console build is justified by a stress-test-only change.

### Recorded five-second timing and bounded-queue model

`tools/check-ps5-native-timing-replay.py` is a second, deliberately optimistic **virtual-time** model using the 68 recorded window durations, actual per-window GPU dispatch sums and actual counts of presented frames. It distributes GPU owner dispatch time uniformly across modeled frame-sized workload units; this is an explicit modeling assumption because source logs do not include each native queue insertion and completion timestamp. With the 32-slot queue held fixed, the baseline 1× load reaches modeled occupancy **1**, and adding one hypothetically GPU-owned pause as long as each window's recorded worst interval (up to **575.264 ms**) reaches occupancy **13**. Neither baseline hypothesis fills the queue. Holding the same modeled service throughput at **4×** and **8×** arrivals fills its capacity (19,058 and 74,720 modeled backpressure events respectively): 32-slot capacity and stop-aware waits are *necessary*, but resizing the queue is not a data-supported fix for observed normal-rate 500 ms stutters.

At zero GPU completion and a hypothetical still-running producer issuing 30 workload units/s, 32 entries would be filled in **1.067 seconds**, far sooner than the measured 1,693.230-second report age; other guest activity can continue meanwhile. **This does not establish whether the actual producer continued attempting submission**, nor whether the GPU owner was itself blocked in a command, a fence, Vulkan presentation, or the detailed profiler. The queue stress, virtual timing replay and real telemetry must remain three distinguishable evidence levels.

Risk matrix for next causal repair: (1) classify the GPU-owner's last real work boundary and producer submission state at initial stall; (2) for transient spikes, compare guest JIT and IPC activity with native per-window delay without mistaking cumulative thread-nanoseconds for serial frame time; (3) keep the game-owned action preferences as an unrelated guest-save/action-resolution problem. **No additional logging flood, queue-capacity change, or blanket thread-priority adjustment is warranted by this source-only replay.**


### 30-FPS-stable gameplay hitches: compositor FPS is not frame freshness

The user reports frequent in-match lag, HUD stutter and delayed gameplay despite **30 FPS remaining stable**. This must **NOT** be conflated with the 500–575 ms presentation gaps during other time windows, or the later full freeze. A post-hoc review of the 68 captured five-second windows finds **36 windows at 29.95–30.05 FPS with worst callback interval below 38 ms** and **all 10 immediately before the prolonged freeze** at approximately 30 FPS with worst callback gap 33.7–38.0 ms.

**Source-level scope error in prior interpretation:** `GraphicsWindow::OnFrameDisplayed()` increments `frame_total` and estimates FPS from end-of-`RendererVulkan::Composite()` callback intervals. On the native Vulkan path the callback is in `SCOPE_EXIT` *after* `present_manager.Present(frame)`; `PresentManager::Present` queues the render frame through `scheduler.Record()` when `async_presentation` is enabled. Native launcher sets `async_presentation = true` for Vulkan; `PresentThread` later performs `CopyToSwapchain`, and the Vulkan present queue is even further downstream. Thus a steady 30 compositor callbacks/s cannot prove a steady 30 actual scanouts/s, stable presentation latency, absence of identical pixel contents, smooth gameplay simulation advancement, or immediate response to controller input. A simulated 120 ms presentation-worker pause **after** the callback is deliberately invisible to this FPS metric.

Guest-side source is also relevant: `HardwareComposer::ComposeLocked` calls `nvdisp.Composite` only when `has_acquired_buffer` becomes true for a **new BufferItem**. Cached held buffers alone do not trigger the callback. Hence stable 30 FPS is useful evidence of new BufferItem acquisition at that cadence. **New BufferItem != new gameplay pose/state != actual TV scanout**. Existing `not_shown=0` also makes a skipped-frame explanation unsupported in this trace.

The 68 detailed source windows include `EDEN_PRESENT_WAIT_PHASE`: `GetRenderFrame` waits for a free present resource total about **0.07 ms per five-second window** (median across consecutive interval deltas) and its preceding completion fence about **0.30 ms** per five-second window; the 32-slot GPU-producer `gpu_full_ms` stays **0** in final normal-rate windows. These figures **argue against persistent** pool exhaustion as the usual source of 30-FPS-visible lag; they do **not** measure `vkQueuePresentKHR`-to-display or distinguish repeated scene content. Guest worker `cpu_ns` clocks were not available on this device trace, so do not infer sustained per-core utilization from them.

The `tools/check-ps5-display-vs-guest-fps.py` offline replay pins all relevant source contracts and uses **150 callbacks in 5 seconds**, projected onto a **60 Hz display**. Host Mac results:

| Deterministic model | Compositor callback FPS | Distinct displayed content states | Longest unchanged interval | p95 display age |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Regular | 30.000 | 150 | 33.33 ms | 33.33 ms |
| Asynchronous present delayed 120 ms intermittently | 30.000 | 150 | 150 ms | 116.67 ms |
| Guest content repeated across otherwise newly acquired frames | 30.000 | 129 | 133.33 ms | 33.33 ms |

A model input just after frame 49 becomes visually observable after **49 ms** in the base case and **149 ms** when the guest's visual state repeats. These are deliberately synthetic clocks/frame identifiers; **they are not measured FC27 input lag or hardware pixel comparisons**.

**Pacing configuration caution:** the Vulkan swapchain implements explicit target-30 pacing, but the engine's default `frame_pacing_mode` is `Target_Auto`. The captured logs do not establish a forced target-30 setting; therefore do **not** claim double limiting or change pacing mode on that assumption. The asynchronous native presentation path is separately source-proven.\n\n**Revised diagnosis priority:** treat two classes as separate incidents. Persistent in-match judder while callback FPS is steady should prioritize the *guest gameplay simulation/action advancement* and *native downstream Vulkan presentation/scanout scheduling*, not keep increasing the GPU command ring, JIT cache or global thread priorities on intuition. The eventual 28-minute no-progress freeze is separately a genuine lack of upstream GPU/tick/frame progress. A single shutdown/stall fix would not automatically cure normal-rate animation judder. Until the guest-state/content identity or true display completion can be established causally, **do not claim a 30-FPS gameplay-hitch fix or request another trial**.


### Source-backed asynchronous presentation and submission-lock stress

**Hardware log facts, unchanged:** 36/68 windows show near-30.0 composite callbacks/s, with worst callback interval below 38 ms, and the last 10 windows are all near 30 FPS before all compositor/GPU counters stop. Native monitor reports a 60 Hz output; most interval histogram counts are the 20–36 ms bucket. No skipped frames were reported. The `EDEN_PRESENT_WAIT_PHASE` total five-second free-buffer-wait and present-frame-fence-wait deltas are tiny in these windows (~0.07 ms and ~0.30 ms), meaning **pool exhaustion was not sustained during the last healthy callbacks**. These counters **do not** observe actual `vkQueuePresentKHR` latency, the display scanout clock, per-buffer scene freshness, or gameplay action advancement.

**Actual compiled C++ source replay:** `tools/check-ps5-async-present-source-stress.py` extracts and compiles the active `PresentManager::GetRenderFrame`, `Present`, `WaitPresent` and `PresentThread` bodies. A host mock scheduler immediately executes the scheduler-record lambda (optimistic), fake fences are nonblocking, and a fake Vulkan present operation injects specified latency. Critically, the native `MAX_FRAMES_IN_FLIGHT=7` is an **upper bound only**. The actual frame pool is `min(swapchain.GetImageCount(), 7)`; the swapchain ordinarily **requests three images**, and the *returned* count is not established by the captured console logs. Accordingly, run both 3- and 7-image pools, not just 7.

| Host scenario (150 callbacks, ~30 FPS) | Maximum callback interval | Maximum downstream present interval | Maximum callback-to-present age |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 present frames, 2 ms nominal | 38.22 ms | 38.22 ms | 5.30 ms |
| **3 present frames, 130 ms intermittent** | **68.37 ms** | 164.42 ms | 132.21 ms |
| **7 present frames, 130 ms intermittent** | **38.38 ms** | 165.82 ms | 135.05 ms |
| 7 present frames, 350 ms intermittent | 152.06 ms | 383.90 ms | 355.07 ms |

Every scenario completed with all 150 frames delivered. The latency thresholds above were checked on the authorized Mac with `EDEN_PRESENT_STRICT_HOST_TIMING=1 python3 -B tools/check-ps5-async-present-source-stress.py`. CI repeats the source-derived lifetime/concurrency run but deliberately does **not** enforce strict wall-clock maxima on shared, potentially overloaded runners; a clean CI run alone cannot validate the 30-FPS timing observations. **This reverses an overbroad earlier conclusion:** a 130 ms present delay can be hidden in the compositor's 30 FPS **when the presentation pool is sufficiently deep**, but **not necessarily when the driver provides only three images**. For the user's final 10 windows (worst compositor callback under 38 ms), repeated 130 ms WSI stalls are a poorer fit if the runtime pool is indeed three. The alternate hypothesis of **new framebuffer buffers carrying stalled/repeated guest animation states** remains viable and is not measurable in current logs. Do not pretend that any Mac simulation establishes the real PS5 image count, game pose updates or scanout cadence.

**Concrete contention dependency:** `Swapchain::Present()` holds `scheduler.submit_mutex` around the actual `present_queue.Present(present_info)` Vulkan call. `Scheduler::SubmitExecution()` takes the *same mutex* around `master_semaphore->SubmitQueue()` on the GPU worker. `tools/check-ps5-vulkan-present-submit-contention.py` anchors both source sites and runs host stand-ins: synthetic presentation holds of **5/130/350 ms** delayed concurrent GPU submission by **5.28/133.39/350.16 ms**, while independent IPC continued. A genuine blocking WSI present could thus couple visible lag to GPU submission pressure, and a driver-side nonreturn could potentially propagate to the prolonged stop. Importantly, this is **a conditional causality model, not evidence that the PS5 WSI driver actually held the lock for 130 ms**.

**Mandatory synchronization warning:** Device setup requests only one Vulkan queue per family and can choose the same family for graphics and present. When the queue handles are identical, Vulkan requires external synchronization of queue use. Removing `submit_mutex` unconditionally is *not a safe fix*. Separately, `Swapchain::AcquireNextImage()` uses `UINT64_MAX` timeout; this is a different potentially indefinite **present-thread** wait that happens *outside* the submit mutex, and can also produce free-pool backpressure. The retrieved native trace cannot distinguish these paths. Never attribute the freeze specifically to the shared lock or the unlimited image acquisition without causal evidence.

**Intervention gate:** do not add per-frame logs or change FIFO vs MAILBOX, timeout handling, priority or queue locking from these host tests alone. The next native change should be a narrowly proved correction with a source-derived preservation test for queue ownership/fence/semaphore order and a rollback contract; no new FC27 console trial from this audit alone.


### First native corrections from source-backed WSI audit

The stress tests make **two Vulkan image-acquisition correctness faults** provable without extrapolating from FPS: (1) when `vkAcquireNextImageKHR` returns `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DATE_KHR`, no valid image index exists, yet the original implementation fell through into `resource_ticks[image_index]` pacing and tick tracking; (2) when it returns `VK_SUBOPTIMAL_KHR`, the acquisition is successful and signals the image-available semaphore, but the original function returned "recreate now" before the acquired image/semaphore was consumed.

Native fix, applied **only** to the generated `vulkan_swapchain.cpp` through `tools/prepare-vulkan-port.py`, not by modifying immutable vendored snapshots:
- `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DATE_KHR`: mark outdated and **return immediately**. Caller uses its existing maximum-three-attempt swapchain recreation path, never an invalid image index.
- `VK_SUBOPTIMAL_KHR`: acquire/present the **valid** current image, allowing its semaphore to be consumed. Preserve the `is_suboptimal` flag; the next `CopyToSwapchainImpl` sees `NeedsRecreation()` and rebuilds the swapchain then, not while the acquired image is unconsumed.
- Native-only `vkAcquireNextImageKHR` waits are changed from `UINT64_MAX` to **40 successive 250ms timeouts (10 seconds total nominal)**. A `VK_TIMEOUT` or `VK_NOT_READY` return is retried without touching image index, resource tick or semaphore state. After 40 exhausted slices throw `vk::Exception(VK_TIMEOUT)`, handled by existing `PresentThread` exception publication and launcher recovery path. This is **bounded failure instead of indefinite wait**, not a hang cure if the underlying driver ignores the timeout; and after a genuine >10-second stall the game will exit via existing failure handling rather than resume.
- All ordinary acquisition success, non-native behavior, fatal surface-loss propagation, queue synchronization and semaphore requirements stay unchanged. The shared `scheduler.submit_mutex` is preserved for identical VkQueue handles. This change does not invent a game animation fix, bypass GPU fences or alter saved game controls.
- `tools/check-ps5-native-acquire-failfast.py` replays **the exact patched body compiled in C++20**, including transient timeout recovery, a run of 40 consecutive timeouts, a no-image/outdated index sentinel, a valid suboptimal image and fatal error propagation. This passes in both native-macro and non-native mode on the authorized Mac. Linux host preflight and native build gate now run the same validation.

**Important validation limit:** A source-level memory/synchronization bug has been corrected; current PS5 telemetry cannot tell whether these two WSI statuses occurred during the recorded 30-FPS hitches. No observed console FPS gain or reduced input lag is claimed. Qualify native build first, then one controlled device comparison only when the code is compiled and ready.

Native qualification gate: compile this exact patched generated swapchain with the All-On native toolchain before claiming it is ready for console validation. The source test only proves the modeled VkResult/error branches; it cannot simulate a WSI driver that ignores Vulkan timeouts.


## Native guest fault — 15 October 2026 (00:45 capture)

The user-supplied capture `boot-trace(20261015-004550).txt`,
`stderr(20261015-004554).log` and `heap(20261015-004550).log`
belongs to tested source `9d066b826cf277efda1f0ea9d5555de18e2f5b08`,
firmware `0x13600007`, title `0100C49025D3E000`.
This is a **specific guest instruction-prefetch fault**, unlike earlier
sessions with a persistent 30-FPS overlay and a stalled GPU-owner heartbeat:

```text
guest thread Job0 tid=90 pc=0x4 lr=0x8b9f42cc
sp=0x10bb46d700 fp=0x10bb46d700 jumped to an unmapped address
```

The guest-fault path also emitted `EDEN_STAGE phase=guest_fault` and
returned to the launcher, not a native signal handler. The heap sample at
the fault reported `failures=0`, `live_bytes=2636901564`, and
`peak_bytes=2856496319`; JIT sparse reservations/commitment were released
during shutdown. None of these observations proves an out-of-memory cause
or JIT corruption. The near-null target `0x4` is consistent with a bad
guest indirect-branch destination, but the saved LR alone cannot identify
who produced it. Do not patch the fault handler to silently continue or
suppress the exception.

Before attempting a correction to guest JIT/HLE, resolve the saved LR
against loaded guest executable segment ranges, and record on the *fault
path only* the instruction/branch source and the relevant register value,
using safe guest-address validation before any memory read. Preserve

zeros cannot be treated as proof that no thread was blocked.


## Cross-check of 01:22 archive — 15 October 2026

The later-collected filenames `boot-trace(20261015-012240).txt`,

Offline numerical analysis of `heap(20261015-012240).log` found 127

The current-session portion of the timestamped network audit (starting

`docs/GPU_DEFERRED_READ_BARRIER_GATE.md`:

```md
# Deferred guest writes: CPU-read and drain-barrier gate

Status: **BLOCKED / not eligible for activation**. Scope: `dev/ps5-sparse-jit`.
Source audit only: no console test, no native SDK compilation, no FPS claim.
The production switch `cpu_write_defer` stays OFF.

## Verified source paths

1. `Core::Memory::Impl::HandleRasterizerWrite` invokes `system.GPU().OnCPUWrite(address, size)`.
   The opt-in bridge preserves `ScopedGuestWriteOrigin` while the Vulkan implementation may enqueue
   the whole invalidation **before** modifying either cache (on buffer mutex contention).
   Guest code may then write the backing RAM immediately.
2. `Core::Memory::Impl::HandleRasterizerDownload` first consults the per-core
   `rasterizer_read_areas` cache. A covered read returns without calling `GPU::OnCPURead`.
3. `GPU::Impl::OnCPURead` consults `RasterizerVulkan::GetFlushArea`. For a
   preemptive area it returns before queuing any GPU request. Otherwise it
   requests `RasterizerVulkan::FlushRegion`, waits on a GPU sync fence, and returns.
   That request does **not** call the deferred queue's `FlushCaching`.
4. The opt-in `Tegra::MemoryManager::FlushCaching` drains queued writes at
   selected GPU commands/engines, but neither CPU-read bypass above has an
   explicit outstanding-write barrier. A read may therefore pass without
   acknowledging an earlier deferred cache invalidation.

Sources:
- `vendor/sources/eden/src/core/memory.cpp`: `HandleRasterizerDownload`, `HandleRasterizerWrite`
- `vendor/sources/eden/src/video_core/gpu.cpp`: `GPU::Impl::OnCPURead`, `RequestSyncOperation`
- `vendor/encore-active/eden-vulkan/vulkan_rasterizer.cpp`: `GetFlushArea`, `FlushRegion`, `OnCPUWrite`
- `headless/guest_write_deferred_bridge.cmake`: opt-in queue, rasterizer and engine wiring
- `headless/gpu_deferred_write_queue.h`: FIFO, unbounded outstanding entries

## Correctness failure mode (not a reproduced game bug)

Deferred invalidation A is accepted while a cache mutex is held. The CPU
subsequently accesses a GPU-tracked range before the GPU owner replays A.
A cached read-area hit can bypass `OnCPURead` entirely; even a non-cached
read can return via `GetFlushArea`'s preemptive shortcut or flush without
draining A first. GPU cache state can therefore lag CPU backing RAM and
read/download ordering is not established. This is a **source-level
counterexample**, not proof that it causes a particular freeze or HUD issue.

## Host-only progress: numbered replay watermark (15 October 2026)

The disabled candidate `headless/gpu_deferred_write_queue.h` now exposes:

- `EnqueueTracked`: monotonically numbered accepted writes, including contiguous
  same-core coalescing, with a per-session total enqueue order.
- `DrainThrough` / `Drain`: GPU-owner callbacks run without the queue mutex;
  the drain is bounded to a captured sequence, even if other producers
  continuously enqueue. A later enqueue from inside a callback remains pending
  for a subsequent drain.
- `CompletedSequence` and `WaitUntil`: a CPU-side waiter can wait for a
  previously accepted ticket. Completion is published only after the
  corresponding replay callback returns. `Close` wakes outstanding readers,
  and rejected writes must never be silently acknowledged.
- `Pending` includes in-flight callbacks, avoiding a false empty indication
  while an older write is being replayed.
- A separate mutex serializes GPU consumers: a second drain waits for the
  earlier replay to finish, then processes its own requested watermark;
  it cannot skip dependent invalidations. Recursive drain of the same queue
  on the owning thread fails fast rather than silently bypassing replay.
  Native lock-order and reentrancy must still be audited before enablement.

Targeted host-only Clang/ASan/UBSan compilation and execution passed (four
producers, 1,280 writes, coalescing, completion wait, shutdown cancellation,
and serialized concurrent replay owners (25 local stress iterations)).
This is **not** a native SDK build and **does not** establish renderer correctness.

**Still missing and blocking:** no real `HandleRasterizerDownload`,
`GPU::OnCPURead` or cache read-area hook uses these tickets, nor does the GPU
command processor schedule a drain on behalf of a waiting reader. `Close`
is not wired into the real title lifecycle. `WaitUntil` without first
scheduling the GPU owner can deadlock, so it must NOT be inserted into the
CPU-read path by itself. There is no safe queue-cap backpressure yet.

A callback completion watermark is NOT a Vulkan device/submit fence. Moreover,
`HandleRasterizerWrite` may enqueue before the actual backing-memory
`memcpy` on the producer returns: native integration must prove the required
CPU payload publication/order relative to GPU reads, not merely mark the
invalidation callback complete. GPU dirty/fence handling and texture
validity remain separate proof obligations.

## Finite replay snapshot: race corrected (source-only)

The earlier `DrainThrough` took a sequence target but repeatedly swapped and
processed the *entire* incoming queue. In the interval between observing the
sequence and acquiring the queue mutex, another producer could append work;
the loop also risked continuing indefinitely under reentrant or constant
concurrent producer pressure.

The corrected code captures **one FIFO snapshot under the queue mutex**,
releases that mutex, then runs all callbacks before publishing the completion
of the last snapshotted entry. New writes after this snapshot remain for a
later GPU-owner boundary. Multiple GPU-owner drainers remain serialized by
`consumer_mutex_`. A ticket passed to `DrainThrough` is therefore a
**minimum completion target**, not an exact maximum: newer entries accepted
*before* the snapshot may be included. That is intentional and host-tested.

A targeted C++20 host reproducer with Clang 17, ASan and UBSan completed 30
iterations covering continual callback enqueues (400 later writes), reader
completion, cancellation at session close and two serialized drain owners.
The repository's `check-gpu-deferred-queue-host.py` now includes an explicit
regression for this bounded snapshot behavior. These checks do not validate
native GPU timing or cache coherency.

## Pre-store publication race: still BLOCKED

The pinned `core/memory.cpp` executes `HandleRasterizerWrite` **before**
writing guest backing memory in `WriteBlockImpl` (tracked `memcpy`),
`ZeroBlock` (`memset`) and the scalar `Write<T>` path. In the disabled
bridge, `HandleRasterizerWrite` may enqueue and return immediately. A GPU
consumer could then replay the cache invalidation, acknowledge the sequence,
and consume RAM **before** the producer completes its actual store. Sequence
tracking cannot repair this fundamental ordering hole.

The bridge therefore also needs a post-store publication protocol that
covers every relevant scalar, exclusive, bulk, zeroing and fastmem write
path, with correct shutdown handling and memory ordering. No consumer may
consider an accepted write replayable until its source payload is published.
The current source-contract test pins the known pre-store ordering as a
**negative gate**, rather than pretending it is safe. Do NOT enable the
bridge or add a GPU read wait solely from the current watermark APIs.

## Two-phase write-publication prototype (host only)

A source-only `Queue::Reserve(core, address, size)` now assigns a FIFO position
**before** the producer changes guest RAM. The returned ticket contains both
a monotonically increasing write sequence and a session generation. Only
`Queue::Publish(ticket)`, called **after the actual guest store**, marks that
entry eligible for GPU-owner replay.

`DrainThrough` snapshots at most the contiguous **published FIFO prefix**;
an earlier unpublished reservation blocks later ready entries even when they
come from a different guest core. Published entries ahead of the first gap
may drain; entries after the gap cannot overtake it. `Publish` releases the
same mutex that a later GPU consumer acquires to snapshot ready work, giving
a C++ happens-before edge from the completed CPU store to the callback.
It **does not** establish a Vulkan completion fence, guest JIT fastmem
publication, or device visibility beyond the host-level callback.

Stale session-generation tickets cannot publish or wait successfully after
`ResetAfterQuiescence`; `Close` prevents new reservations and releases
waiters. A missed `Publish` intentionally leaves an unresolved FIFO entry
until shutdown instead of silently replaying uncommitted RAM.

**Native opt-in bridge is still NOT wired to this protocol.** Its generated
`MemoryManager::EnqueueDeferredCPUWrite` still calls the eager
`deferred_cpu_write_queue.Enqueue` before the guest's actual store.
A fail-closed host source test pins this mismatch; it must be replaced with
a real post-store integration across scalar, exclusive, zero, block and JIT
fastmem write paths before `cpu_write_defer` could ever be enabled.
No console build or on-device test is justified by this host prototype.

**Remaining liveness problem:** native `GPU::OnCPURead` and
`HandleRasterizerDownload` can bypass queue drainage. A read waiting
for a reserved ticket also requires scheduling the GPU owner after publish;
there is no such native orchestration yet. Native shutdown/wakeup and
queue pressure constraints remain unqualified.

## Native runtime interlock and write-site inventory (15 October 2026)

The experimental source generation previously retained a dangerous escape
hatch: even with the default switch OFF, a future runtime toggle could have
entered the legacy eager `Enqueue` before the guest's actual `memcpy` or
`memset` completed. The native bridge now checks the compile-time
`kNativePostStorePublicationReady = false` guard at BOTH the candidate
rasterizer path and the enqueue helper. With the guard false, a cache-mutex
contention uses the original blocking path rather than deferring it.
This protects the currently unqualified opt-in developer configuration even
if someone accidentally changes `cpu_write_defer` at runtime. Flipping the
guard is prohibited until the checklist below is met.

The pinned `core/memory.cpp` has **eight** `HandleRasterizerWrite`
references (seven call sites plus the definition):

| Write source | Current action | Publication risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WriteBlockImpl` | Callback before tracked `memcpy` | Pre-store |
| `ZeroBlock` | Callback before tracked `memset` | Pre-store |
| Scalar `Write<T>` | Callback during pointer lookup, then `memcpy` | Pre-store |
| `WriteExclusive<T>` | Callback before atomic compare/exchange | May not store |
| `WriteExclusive128` | Callback before 128-bit compare/exchange | May not store |
| `StoreDataCache` | Cache operation; no direct store in the callback | Already-written data; ordering must be proven |
| `FlushDataCache` | Cache operation; no direct store in the callback | Already-written data; ordering must be proven |

`CopyBlock` routes its writes through `WriteBlockImpl` and can perform
a preceding `HandleRasterizerDownload`. Other device-pointer, JIT/fastmem
and write-watch paths need separate verification; the list is an audit of
**this file's dispatch sites**, not proof that all writers are covered.

Before enabling native deferral: wrap each actual data-producing operation
with a reservation whose ticket is published only after its store has
completed; accommodate conditional atomic success, CPU cache operations,
and multiple nested or split writes. Prove that no untracked GPU/cache
writer can enter the deferred path, and do not change the CPU-read barrier
until GPU-thread scheduling and session lifetime are proven separately.

## Session identity is mandatory for read waits and drains

Host tests exposed an ambiguity in the first two-phase queue API: plain
`Sequence` values restart from 1 after title teardown. A consumer holding
sequence 1 from the old title could accidentally wait on, or drain, sequence
1 in the new title. The queue now returns a `Ticket {sequence, generation}`
from both `Reserve` and `EnqueueTracked`, accepts only a ticket for
`WaitUntil` and `DrainThrough`, and rejects a ticket whose generation
does not match the current session. Bare-number waits and drains are
rejected at C++ compile time by the host fixture. `Drain()` internally
captures the queue's current generation and accepted watermark.

This prevents one specific class of stale-session API misuse. The
`ResetAfterQuiescence` lifecycle precondition remains mandatory, and
neither a completed ticket nor a flush request proves GPU device-fence
completion. No native CPU reader has been wired to these APIs; the
`kNativePostStorePublicationReady = false` interlock remains in force.

## Cross-address-space ticket isolation

A further host audit found that the first generation-tagged API initialized
each Queue's `generation_` to 1. Distinct guest address spaces could thus
both issue `Ticket{1, 1}`, allowing one queue's ticket to be accepted by
another. Each Queue instance and each quiescent reset now acquires a fresh,
process-unique epoch from a checked atomic counter. Ticket identity therefore
covers the owning address space and the title session, in addition to FIFO
order. The host fixture tests rejection of foreign tickets on Publish,
WaitUntil and DrainThrough; bare sequence waits/drains remain unsupported.

This is a narrow host-level correctness proof, not an authorization to
activate the deferred path. GPU work scheduling, post-store native producer
integration, page-mapping lifetime and cache/texture fence ordering still
need separate verification.

## Shutdown replay lifetime barrier

A source audit found that merely setting `closed_` and waking the waiting
CPU threads allowed an already-entered `DrainThrough` callback to continue
after `Close()` returned. A title could then tear down rasterizer/texture
resources while a GPU-owner callback was still using them.

The inactive queue's `Close()` now performs three ordered steps:

1. Under the queue mutex, set `closed_` so new reservations, publications
   and new GPU drain snapshots are rejected.
2. Wake outstanding CPU waiters without holding the GPU-consumer lock.
3. Acquire the GPU-consumer mutex **after releasing the queue mutex** and wait
   for any already-active GPU replay batch to finish before returning.

The host fixture coordinates an active blocked GPU callback, a CPU waiter
and a closing thread. It asserts that the reader is cancelled promptly but
`Close()` cannot finish until that callback completes. A separate test
asserts that queued writes are not replayed after closure.

**Strict native integration preconditions:** `Close()` must not run from
inside a replay callback and must never be called while the caller holds a
GPU cache lock needed by that callback. All producers and waiters must be
joined before deleting the owning queue and address-space structures. A
callback that itself blocks indefinitely may delay closure indefinitely;
the host test verifies ordering, not shutdown progress for every engine
deadlock scenario. This is **not** a lifecycle integration into the native
title manager and does not make the bridge eligible for activation.

## Partial replay exception: poison instead of false completion

The inactive queue formerly removed a published batch from its FIFO before
invoking the rasterizer. A C++ exception from an individual replay callback
would then destroy that batch without advancing its completion watermark.
Subsequent drain attempts could process newer writes despite older, partially
applied cache operations being missing.

The queue now catches callback exceptions only to **poison the owning title
session**, wake pending CPU readers, and rethrow the original exception.
While poisoned:

- no later GPU drain can run, even after the throwing callback exits;
- no new writes may be enqueued or published;
- outstanding `WaitUntil(ticket)` calls fail rather than hang;
- the failed batch is **not** acknowledged as replayed;
- `Pending()` remains true until quiescent teardown, and `Failed()` exposes
  the terminal state for diagnostics.

A callback may already have changed buffer/texture state before throwing,
so blindly retrying that item would not be safe or necessarily idempotent.
The generated developer-only `MemoryManager::FlushCaching` now also checks
`Queue::Failed()` and terminates rather than allowing a later GPU command to
continue with the poisoned cache state, even if an intermediate layer catches
the original exception. This is a fail-closed safety gate, **not crash
recovery**, and the developer bridge remains disabled.
Only `Close()`, joining the producers/readers/GPU consumer and
`ResetAfterQuiescence()` can clear the poison for a *new* title session.
This is **not a runtime recovery mechanism**. Callers must treat a poison
as a fatal per-session coherency failure and avoid submitting more GPU work.

The C++ host sanitizer fixture now throws during the second callback in a
batch, verifies the exception reaches its caller, the reader is released
with failure and no fresh write/replay is accepted, then resets after joining
all threads. It does not model Vulkan's partially applied cache operations.

## Quiescent reset is now a checked lifecycle transition

The queue previously allowed `ResetAfterQuiescence()` while the session
was still open, simply trusting the caller's promise that all producers and
GPU callbacks had stopped. That could clear in-flight ticket state and
recycle the queue for a new title while old work was still active.

`ResetAfterQuiescence()` now returns `false` unless `Close()` has
**fully completed**, not merely set the close flag. It first acquires the
GPU-consumer mutex (except from inside its own callback, where it refuses
to proceed), then the queue mutex, preserving the established lock order.
A successful reset clears the completed-close gate, discards old-session
state and issues a fresh process-unique epoch for new tickets.

This protects against accidental live-session resets. The caller must
**still join all producers, CPU read waiters and GPU consumers before reset**;
that external ownership/lifetime rule is not automatically provable from
queue-local locks. Reset is not designed to race a second `Close()` call.

The host regression rejects reset on an open session or inside a replay
callback, and requires close-before-reset on all previous fixture paths.
The native bridge is still disabled and does not yet manage this lifecycle.

## Host backlog: publication lookup no longer quadratic

The queue's `Publish(ticket)` previously linearly scanned every pending
write, while another CPU core could publish a later reservation before an
earlier one. A backlog of `n` separate reservations published in reverse
order therefore required up to O(n²) comparisons just to mark them ready,
before any rasterizer work.

The queue already assigns strictly increasing `last_sequence` values to
FIFO entries. Same-core coalescing only changes the final entry's upper
sequence; GPU draining removes a prefix without reordering survivors.
`Publish` now performs a `std::lower_bound` lookup on this monotone key
under the existing queue mutex, giving O(log n) search with identical
exact-ticket and unpublished-entry validation.

The host fixture adds 4,096 reserved writes published in reverse order,
then verifies zero premature replay and exact FIFO output. It also tests
publication after a previously published prefix has been drained, including
rejecting the removed ticket. The source contract pins binary lookup.

This reduces one potential CPU contention hotspot in the **inactive
prototype**, not the native GPU rendering cost. The unbounded queue's
memory pressure, repeated prefix vector moves, guest-write publication,
GPU-read barriers and session integration remain blockers to activation.

## Lost GPU wake after publication: source-only scheduling contract

In the source-proven GPU path, `Core::Memory::HandleRasterizerDownload`
may return early from its per-core read-area cache, and
`GPU::Impl::OnCPURead` may return on a preemptive `GetFlushArea`.
Neither schedules a deferred queue drain. A pending `Reserve` can thus
make a GPU owner's `Drain()` return zero; simply publishing that entry
later does not, by itself, cause any GPU thread to revisit the queue.

The host-only queue now provides `PublishAndWake(ticket, request_gpu)`:

1. Validate the generation-tagged ticket and publish the completed RAM store
   under the queue mutex, using binary search over sequence-ordered writes.
2. Recognize an **edge from an unready FIFO head to a published head**.
   Publishing a tail behind an unpublished head does not spuriously wake the
   GPU. A newly published former head does, including after a preceding
   prefix was already drained.
3. Release the queue mutex **before** invoking the caller-supplied
   `request_gpu()` callback. A synchronous host test demonstrates the
   callback can reenter the queue without a lock inversion; in the native
   engine the callback must normally **enqueue GPU-thread work**, not
   recursively perform rasterizer replay on the GPU-owner thread.
4. If the scheduling callback throws, poison the title's queue and release
   blocked readers with an error. Do not claim the write has been replayed
   or rely on an unrelated later draw to repair the broken ordering.

The host fixture covers an initially blocked GPU drain, reverse publication
of 256 writes with **one** GPU wake, a published prefix followed by a
previously unpublished hole and a second wake, and scheduling failure.
It also holds a producer inside its GPU scheduling callback while title
`Close()` runs: the CPU read waiter is released, but the close operation
cannot return until the callback exits. Wake-callback lifetime is counted
under the queue mutex **before** invoking the notifier, and `Close()`
waits on a separate condition variable for all counted wake callbacks.
This protects the caller from reclaiming GPU scheduler resources while an
earlier producer is still issuing a GPU wake. A scheduling callback that
blocks forever will delay closure, so the eventual native implementation
must supply a nonblocking, bounded-lifetime wake request.
The fixture now also runs a separate asynchronous host GPU worker: its
first callback deliberately remains in progress while two later reservations
publish out of order. The wake request generated by the previously blocked
head must survive that in-flight callback and cause a second GPU-owner drain,
with exactly ordered replay and no duplicate ranges. The host-only queue
rejects recursive `Close()` from its own wake callback to avoid waiting for
itself to finish. These are host protocol checks, not native renderer results.

**This is not yet wired to any native post-store write path.** The current
developer-only bridge still uses eager `Enqueue` and the
`kNativePostStorePublicationReady = false` interlock. Future production
integration must schedule work safely on the existing
`GPU::Impl::RequestSyncOperation` / `gpu_thread.TickGPU` path, ensure
asynchronous/synchronous GPU modes and shutdown are handled, avoid holding
buffer/texture locks, and run all read barriers against *published* writes
before their CPU reader proceeds. Producer lifecycle must keep the queue
and GPU scheduler alive through the wake callback. A wake is not a
Vulkan fence and must not be mistaken for completion.

## Fail-closed CPU read tickets during shutdown

The original `WaitUntil(ticket)` woke readers when a session was closed or
poisoned, but returned success whenever the sequence watermark had been
completed. A GPU replay callback finishing concurrently with `Close()`,
or a previous successful callback followed by a replay exception, could
therefore make an unusable title's CPU reader believe its cache state was
still valid.

The host-only queue now requires **both** successful replay completion
**and** a live, unpoisoned session at the return point of `WaitUntil`.
A closed or failed session cannot authorize further CPU reads, even for
tickets acknowledged earlier. Host regressions cover an in-flight callback
completed during teardown, a completed write followed by `Close()`,
and a previously successful write followed by a later poisoned callback.

This does not prove guest-side visibility or Vulkan barriers, and the
developer-only bridge remains disabled. A native reader must treat `false`
as a fatal/session-cancelled barrier outcome rather than continuing with
potentially stale RAM.

## Bounded pending write budget

An uncommitted FIFO reservation blocks replay of every later reservation.
Previously, producers could continue accepting guest writes without any
limit while that head was unready, risking unbounded per-title memory
growth. The inactive queue now admits at most **8,192 accepted but not yet
acknowledged writes**, calculated as `accepted_ - completed_` under the
queue mutex. This includes:

- published or unpublished writes sitting in the FIFO;
- an entire GPU snapshot currently inside a replay callback (removed from
  the vector but not yet acknowledged);
- separately accepted sequence IDs merged into a single eager tail entry.

At the limit, both `Reserve` and legacy `EnqueueTracked` reject new
writes without advancing a sequence. Existing reserved writes can still
`Publish` and drain normally; once replay completes, the budget opens
again. The host test fills all 8,192 slots behind an unpublished head,
publishes them in reverse order, checks replay order and attempts a new
reservation from inside the still-in-flight GPU callback. It also verifies
that eager same-range coalescing cannot bypass the budget.

**Critical integration contract:** a rejected `Reserve` is not an
acknowledgment and must cause the actual CPU write site to take an original
synchronous/cache-correct path *before storing guest RAM*, or fail the
session. A caller must never drop the invalidation and continue. This
host-only bound does not prove any FPS gain, and the native developer bridge
remains disabled while its pre-store enqueue is unqualified.

## Native GPU worker failure versus CPU sync-fence liveness

A separate audit of the **active native GPU worker** found a concrete
failure mode independent of the disabled deferred guest-write queue. The
native worker already catches exceptions, records an `exception_ptr` via
`Eden::RecordGpuFailure`, and requests its stop token. However,
`GPU::Impl::WaitForSyncOperation(fence)` traditionally waits on
`sync_request_cv` until the GPU-owned `TickWork()` increments the
completion fence. Once the worker has exited unexpectedly, no subsequent
`TickWork()` can acknowledge outstanding requests. The deliberate
`NotifyShutdown()` path cancels waits **after joining the GPU worker**,
but a CPU thread blocked on a missing fence might prevent the shutdown
sequence from starting.

The native build now derives `gpu.cpp` with a source-pinned
`headless/gpu_sync_failure_wait.inc` method. It preserves the original
condition-variable completion notification and shutdown cancellation, but
checks a non-consuming copy of the already recorded fatal GPU error at
most every 100 ms while a fence is pending. On failure it rethrows that
original exception, rather than letting the CPU reader hang or inventing
fence completion. Multiple readers can observe the same fatal event;
`TakeGpuFailure` still clears the error only when a new GPU worker starts.

`tools/check-gpu-sync-failure-host.py` reproduces the actual native
CMake source-generation fragment and compiles the resulting wait method
with host ASan/UBSan. It tests immediate normal completion,
two separate CPU waiters observing one unconsumed fatal worker error, and
unchanged voluntary shutdown cancellation without falsely advancing a
fence. The host workflow runs this test without building a console app.

The same native `GPU::Impl::TickWork` callback loop previously called
`sync_request_mutex.unlock()` directly while its `std::unique_lock lck`
still reported ownership. If `request()` threw, stack unwinding would
call the lock destructor while the mutex was already unlocked, invoking
undefined behaviour. The native derivation now uses `lck.unlock()` and
`lck.lock()`, so the guard tracks the actual ownership. The host fixture
executes the derived `TickWork` in normal and throwing-callback cases,
verifies the mutex is reusable after the error, and retains the original
fence completion rules.

This is a **fatal-error liveness correction in the native runtime**, not
a verified FC27 performance or gameplay fix. A GPU worker that remains
alive but blocks inside a rasterizer command will not record an exception;
the guard therefore does not address GPU work deadlocks, missing guest
fences, or all observed freezes. It also does not enable the deferred
guest-write queue, whose post-store native contract remains incomplete.

## Required engineering contract

- Give accepted entries an ordered, per-session completion watermark.
  A read of a tracked range must observe the completion of every
  causally earlier conflicting write before relying on cached read areas
  or calculating/flushing the GPU download area. Cross-core ordering is
  assigned by the queue's mutex, not by host thread identity.
- Put the read dependency check **before the per-core cached-area shortcut**
  and the `GetFlushArea` shortcut; patching only `GPU::OnCPURead` is insufficient.
- Request GPU-owner drainage and wait for its acknowledged watermark.
  No CPU caller may replay GPU cache operations directly. Do not wait
  while holding a GPU buffer/texture cache mutex or the queue mutex.
- Cover each live graphics address space, including non-default channels;
  the queue lives in a `Tegra::MemoryManager`, not a process-global singleton.
- Replace any future queue cap with watermark-aware drainage and
  shutdown-aware backpressure. Never fall back to synchronous handling
  of a newer write while older writes remain pending.
- At title shutdown/switch, either complete all required work before
  destroying caches/queues or explicitly cancel after producer quiescence;
  no blocked CPU producer or dangling GPU callback may survive teardown.

## Required host/native qualification before any console test

1. **Deterministic order test:** enqueue A, trigger a read before draw/DMA,
   assert replay completion precedes read-area lookup and GPU download.
2. **Read shortcut test:** already-cached read area and preemptive
   `GetFlushArea` both still honor pending write dependencies.
3. **Concurrency test:** four guest producers, overlapping ranges, GPU
   owner drainage, reads racing with writes; no lost or reordered
   pre-watermark invalidations.
4. **Liveness test:** a full queue blocks producers only outside locks;
   GPU drain unblocks them; cancellation during shutdown releases waiters;
   continuous producers cannot indefinitely starve the GPU owner.
5. **Native test:** compile the ON development bridge with the actual native
   toolchain and linked source units, then inspect real call ordering.
   Host source fixtures and sanitizers alone do not satisfy this gate.

The previous host run `38794257575` validates its listed host checks only.
Neither that run nor upstream experimental patches establish this read barrier.
Keep `EDEN_GUEST_WRITE_BRIDGE_DEV` and `cpu_write_defer` OFF for shipping.

# Encore integration audit — CPU/HLE, GPU, JIT and memory

Date: **14 October 2026**. Single target branch: `dev/ps5-sparse-jit`.
This is a **source-path and build-selection audit** against concrete upstream sources.
It is not a statement that every upstream commit in every related repository
has been reviewed or that an improvement in FC27 gameplay has been measured.

## Critical distinction: runtime vs repository presence

A feature is not integrated merely because a file exists in
`vendor/sources` or `vendor/encore-active`. The build must select the source,
its relevant feature flag must be enabled, a native candidate must compile and
link, and gameplay behavior must then be verified on device. The inventory
of 22/22 dependencies in `UPSTREAM_GAP_REGISTER_2026-10-14.md` is **not**
a list of 22 complete functional upstream backports.

## Source and production status

| Priority | Feature and source | Encore status | Evidence and remaining verification |

This eliminates that **source-level ownership violation** but does **not** prove console compilation or fix FC27 gameplay. |

Main ProsperoEden sets `EDEN_SHARED_JIT ON` on native/Linux. This is a **deliberate stability divergence**; tests of these dormant classes do not establish production performance. |

The newer `EDEN_GUEST_CACHE_LOCK_TAIL` observes >1 ms and >10 ms waits without removing locks; no fresh real-game trace has established its actual long-tail distribution. |

## Why our previous conclusion was too strong

The latest available 415-window match telemetry is from `2efd8b3c`,
not from the new modifications. It documents 858 frames >50 ms, 10 >500 ms,
and a prolonged content/progression stall while the compositor stays active.
It **cannot** establish whether later source changes improved or worsened FC27.
The host/GPU stress replays prove bounded queues preserve behavior under
synthetic load, not that in-game frames or saved controls progress correctly.

The latest native diagnostic run `38545198780` **failed to compile** in
`headless/performance.cpp` (attempted atomic `exchange()` on a const
counter). Commit `aac065ab6045e8a3ce90d2cfb09eeb08c0c8a6cf`
changes this to a mutable local reference. The fix is **source-corrected but
not yet validated by a successful native run for that SHA**. No claims of a
new green console candidate should be made for this particular change.

## Priorities and qualifying gates

1. **CPU/HLE — actual guest progress and synchronization.**
   Capture wait reason and owner/callee for title threads around the freeze.
   Counter increments for IPC and draws are not proof of game progress. Keep
   lock ABI unchanged unless trace shows a specific waiting cycle.
2. **GPU — in-game content freshness, cache and shader cold starts.**
   Correlate >50 ms frames with buffer lock outliers, shader pipeline
   compilation/first-use, and GPU fence waits. Distinguish generated content
   versions from frame presentation counts. Verify **actual Mesa disk cache
   activation** before changing rendering or process privileges.
3. **JIT — classifying costs before new compilation strategies.**
   Record per-core JIT compile counts/durations, page commits, cache
   evacuations and generated block hotness. Compare startup (<6k frames)
   against sustained gameplay (6k–32k). Do not mistake a window's JIT time
   for a single frame's stall.
4. **Potential adaptive compilation — only as an isolated experiment.**
   Keep ordinary Dynarmic stable. On an independently built development
   variant, measure baseline block compilation first; then evaluate a
   two-tier policy (fast cold compile, bounded background optimization of
   hot blocks) with immutable build flags and strict eviction/invalidation
   and resource limits. Cross-core shared compilation and asynchronous
   code patching need fresh concurrency and executable-alias validation;
   neither can be activated merely because Java has a tiered JIT.
5. **Memory — qualified subsystem changes, not one giant cherry-pick.**
   Compare guest lazy backing, JIT incremental code commitment, sparse page
   tables and free direct/flexible memory independently. Preserve fail-closed
   startup and per-page alias lifetime guarantees.

**Integration audit limitation:** this inspection compares named high-impact
source locations and production wiring; it is *not* a file-by-file evaluation
of every commit in every external repository previously discussed (including
independent experimental forks). The upstream gap register documents divergent
Mesa and SDK histories, and GitHub changed-file results may be truncated.
No FC27 save data or console file was read or modified.

## Corrected native cache integration audit

**Correction to the earlier conclusion:** the plain pinned Mesa code requires
`geteuid()==getuid()` and `getegid()==getgid()` before accepting disk
caching. But Encore does **not** compile that unmodified policy on PS5.
Its actual production source
`vendor/encore-active/ps5-mesa/src/util/disk_cache_os.c` includes a
selective `#if !defined(__PROSPERO__)` guard around the
`__normal_user()` rejection. That adaptation was already present, came
from `mpereiraesaa/PS5_Mesa`, and is proved against the immutable source by
`tools/check-ps5-mesa-shader-cache.py` (including native/host C sanitizers).
Changing the process group via `setegid(getgid())` is **not** an identified
missing correction for Encore. The earlier claim based only on
`vendor/sources/ps5-mesa` was mistaken.

The new one-time `EDEN_GPU_DISK_CACHE_CONTEXT` marker logs UID/GID match
flags, cache-directory presence and existence of a disable environment
variable. On this driver, mismatch alone is **not** interpreted as a cache
rejection. The parser `tools/check-native-shader-cache-eligibility.py`
checks the exact native source bypass, treats absent events as
**NOT_MEASURED**, and never claims shader cache hits from the configuration.
It makes **no credential change or filesystem mutation**.

The `2efd8b3c` capture only contains
`EDEN_RADV_DISK_CACHE limit_mib=2048 free_mib=16384`, which cannot
confirm shader cache hit rate. A genuine shader hit/miss or cache-file
reuse probe is still needed if shader compilation remains a bottleneck.

Build qualification: run `38547995294` completed successfully and
uploaded the native test package and symbols before the new context
marker. The later marker must pass its own source preflight and native
compilation; there are no new console performance measurements.

## Lessons for the upstream adaptation audit

Never infer what Encore runs solely from the original immutable
`vendor/sources/` snapshot. For each relevant fix, compare
**original source → `vendor/encore-active/` compiled source → concrete
CMake/native build path → source/host test → runtime trace**. In this
case the existing test `check-ps5-mesa-shader-cache.py` was stronger
evidence than either the documentation or the original Mesa source.


## Full native graphics archive provenance (follow-up)

A second source-to-binary integration gap was found in the build scripts.
The original native archive reuse check in `tools/prepare-build.sh` checked
only the pinned Mesa revision and the adapted **WSI** source hash
(`EDEN_WSI_SHA256`). It did not compare the other ten patched Mesa inputs,
including `src/util/disk_cache_os.c`. Thus an archive could be linkable but
still contain an outdated translation unit even while the source tests passed.

The corrected build now fingerprints **all eleven** maintained files listed
by `tools/install-vendored-radv.py::PATHS`; the deterministic SHA256
includes relative paths, lengths and file digests. Only the second,
successful native driver compilation can write
`EDEN_ACTIVE_INPUTS_SHA256`, after verifying every staged source matches
the maintained tree. Missing or mismatched stamps force regeneration and
discard any old isolated archive. `tools/radv-active-inputs.py --self-test`
individually mutates each of the 11 paths to prove all invalidate reuse.

Also, `install-vendored-radv.py` now refreshes the modified file's mtime
after atomic replacement. Preserving the *original* source mtime with
`copy2` could make an older source file appear older than Ninja's
compiled object, preventing recompilation even after bytes changed.
`check-vendored-radv-fork.py` now verifies the actual post-install mtime
change with a deliberately stale test input.

This **strengthens compiled-source selection**, not emulator performance.
The first cold reconstruction of the native driver may be slower. No new
FC27 match demonstrates any FPS or texture change, and the new source
fingerprint guard still requires CI and native build qualification.
